title: Basic Prompting for Code
description: Master the fundamentals of writing clear, effective prompts for AI coding assistants.

data.text: The Golden Rule: Context Is Everything

The single biggest factor in the quality of AI-generated code is the amount and quality of context you provide. An AI model has no knowledge of your project, your team's conventions, your existing codebase, or your personal preferences — unless you tell it.

data.title: The context sandwich
data.text: Structure your prompt like a sandwich: top slice is the goal and constraints, the filling is the relevant code or examples, and the bottom slice is the expected output format. This gives the AI everything it needs to generate useful code.

data.title: Always include when asking for code:
items: The language and framework you are using (React 18 with TypeScript, not just "React")
The relevant file contents or a description of the current state
The expected behavior in plain English
Any constraints (must use a specific library, must be under 50 lines, etc.)
An example of the input and expected output if applicable

data.title: Use this structure for consistently better results:
items: Role: "You are an expert in [language/framework]" — sets expectations
Task: The specific code task — write a function, fix a bug, explain a pattern
Context: The surrounding code, file paths, or architecture notes
Constraints: Libraries to use, style requirements, performance needs
Example: Input/output pair if the task is data transformation
Output format: "Return only the function, with comments" or "Explain step by step"

data.title: Mistakes that produce worse code:
items: "Write a function" without specifying inputs, outputs, or edge cases
Asking for a complete implementation when you actually need a single utility
Giving the AI a 2,000-line file with no indication of which part matters
Not specifying the language version (Python 3.10+ vs 3.6 changes available features)
Forgetting to mention the testing framework or linting rules your project uses

data.title: Bad prompt vs. good prompt
data.content:
Bad: "Write a fetch function"

Good: "Write a TypeScript fetch wrapper function called apiGet<T> that takes a URL and optional headers, returns a Promise<T>, handles HTTP errors by throwing, and uses the project's existing AuthService for the Authorization header. Use the project's ApiError class for error responses. Follow the existing pattern in src/utils/http.ts."

data.text: Rarely will your first prompt produce perfect code. The most effective workflow is iterative: ask for an initial version, review the output, then refine with specific follow-up prompts. "Now add input validation for empty strings" or "Refactor this to use async/await" are examples of productive follow-up prompts.

data.title: Iterate, do not start over
data.text: Each follow-up prompt builds on the previous context. Instead of pasting a new prompt from scratch, continue the conversation. The AI retains the code it already generated and can modify it directly.
When to Switch to Chat Mode

If your task is complex enough that you need to ask clarifying questions, switch from inline completion to a chat interface. Chat allows you to show larger code blocks, ask for explanations, and iterate through multiple revisions in one conversation. Use inline completion for quick single-line suggestions and chat for anything requiring discussion.

I included the relevant code or described the current state
I stated the expected behavior in plain English
I mentioned any constraints (libraries, line limits, style)
I provided an example of input/output if applicable
